title: Solana Policy Institute Asks SEC for Control-Based Ledger Test
description: The Solana Policy Institute asked the SEC to define permissionless ledgers for tokenized-stock venues through five control and access factors.
why_it_matters: The requested guidance could affect which blockchain architectures tokenized securities venues can use under the SEC exemption, making network governance a compliance design issue rather than only a technical choice.
keyTakeaways: The Solana Policy Institute asked the SEC to use a functional, control-based definition of a public, permissionless ledger.
Its proposed five-factor test covers open-source code, transaction access, transparent rules and concentrated authority over validation, inclusion, finality or censorship.
The letter is a policy request, not SEC guidance or a change to the existing exemption.
body:
The Solana Policy Institute asked the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to clarify what qualifies as a public, permissionless distributed ledger for tokenized securities venues. Its October 22 comment supports a functional, control-based standard rather than a prescribed network architecture.

The group proposed five considerations: open-source code; open reading and transaction submission; execution under pre-established transparent rules; whether one person or controlled group has persistent authority over sequencing, validation, inclusion, finality or consensus changes; and whether anyone can unilaterally censor use or receive preferential permissions.

The letter also says temporary, disclosed incident-response measures should not automatically disqualify a network. These are recommendations from an industry policy group, not SEC guidance, an approval or a change to the exemption.

sources.name: Solana Policy Institute — SEC comment letter

facts.claim: The institute asked the SEC to define permissionless ledgers through a functional test focused on control.
The letter says the existing exemption does not define public, permissionless distributed ledger.
The proposed factors include whether a ledger's protocol and underlying code are fully open source.
The proposed test asks whether transactions execute under pre-established and transparent protocol rules.
The institute says disclosed incident-response powers should be temporary and limited to addressing the incident.
